subject: Cooking
title: Vital Wheat Gluten: The Protein Powder of Bread
description: A 60-second lesson on Vital Wheat Gluten: The Protein Powder of Bread.

hook.text: You can buy pure gluten as a powder and add it to any flour. Bakers use it to rescue weak doughs.

buildup.text: Vital wheat gluten is made by washing flour dough until all starch is removed — leaving only protein.

discovery.text: Adding 1–2 tablespoons to whole wheat flour compensates for the bran that cuts gluten strands.

twist.text: Seitan — the Buddhist vegetarian meat — is pure wheat gluten, seasoned and cooked. It's 75% protein.

climax.text: Gluten went from bread ingredient to meat substitute — a 1,500-year-old Chinese invention now in Western supermarkets.

punchline.text: The same protein that raises bread also replaces steak.

details.summary: Vital wheat gluten is pure dried gluten protein extracted from wheat flour, used to boost the protein content and rise of whole grain and gluten-free-blended breads. Adding one to two tablespoons per cup of flour strengthens weak doughs.
details.whyItMatters: Vital wheat gluten solves the structural weakness of whole grain, rye, and ancient grain breads without changing their character. It also enables seitan production for plant-based diets.
takeaways: Pure gluten protein boosts dough strength in weak flour blends
One to two tablespoons per cup of flour improves whole grain rise
Seitan is made primarily from vital wheat gluten and water

faq.question: When should you add vital wheat gluten to bread dough?
faq.answer: Add it when using low-protein flours like whole wheat, rye, spelt, or ancient grains that produce weak gluten networks. Mix it directly into the dry flour before adding water. One to two tablespoons per cup of flour is sufficient. It is unnecessary with strong bread flour.

faq.question: What is seitan and how is it made from vital wheat gluten?
faq.answer: Seitan is vital wheat gluten mixed with water and seasonings, kneaded until elastic, then simmered or steamed. The result has a chewy, meat-like texture with about 25 grams of protein per serving. It has been a protein source in Asian cuisines for over a thousand years.
